May include study of intervention theories and models; analysis of change strategies across individual, group, organizational and community contexts; consideration of message design, persuasion and implementation; exploration of needs assessment, behavior change frameworks, action research, dialogic approaches, training design and evaluation models. Examples may draw from campaigns, organizations, communities, public initiatives and/or social or institutional problem-solving.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines key concepts and theories for understanding how people create, maintain and sometimes challenge relationships through communication. Considers person-to-person and online interaction, including perception, attraction, self-disclosure, listening and/or conflict management. Explores communication across interpersonal differences such as professional and social roles, class, age, ability, gender, race, ethnicity, sexuality, nationality and religion. Examines practices for analyzing interpersonal communication through research and theory. Course materials may include consideration of diverse perspectives and examples of communication as both productive and destructive, in face-to-face and online contexts. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds skills for effective interaction in personal, professional and civic settings. Develops tools for effective listening, conflict management and resolution and adapting to others from diverse backgrounds and perspectives. Supports understanding of how interpersonal communication influences health, well-being and quality of life. Builds academic preparation for advanced study and workforce preparation for careers requiring teamwork, leadership and strong relational and collaborative competence. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday ideas about relationships and communication may differ from research-based perspectives. Considers ways that listening involves more than paying attention, that conflict can strengthen as well as weaken relationships and reasons disclosure and trust do not always follow predictable stages. Builds recognition of how identity, culture and context shape meaningful interactions, showing ways communication approaches that seem natural in one setting may be interpreted differently or counter-productively in another. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of perception, attraction, self-disclosure, listening and conflict management; study of interaction patterns and stages in relationship development; analysis of communication across interpersonal dimensions such as gender, race, ethnicity, sexuality, social class, ability, nationality and religion; consideration of productive and destructive aspects of communication; application of interpersonal theory to face-to-face and online contexts, including social media.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: Examine the role of media and its impact on human behavior, emotions and thoughts; topics include mass media, social media and how they influence individual and societal functioning across a range of important psychological topics; e.g., self-image, sexual behavior, mental health, violence.
prerequisites: PBSI 107.

description: Laws and regulations applied to social media, including communication law applied to enduring issues in the social media context; legal problems unique to social media; free speech, commercial speech and employment law as they affect individual users of social media as well as groups and organizations promoting points of view or products via social media, and employers.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the study of communication within organizational contexts, with attention to how messages, relationships and structures constitute organizations and shape organizational life. Surveys foundational theories and contemporary perspectives on how communication influences organizing, including attention to practices associated with collective identity-building, leadership, decision-making, culture, power, technology use and/or change. Examines how communication enables coordination across teams and influences how people experience belonging, authority or conflict in organizational life. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds workforce preparation for professional contexts where collaboration, leadership and organizational activities depend on communication across roles, departments and demographic or cultural differences. Promotes effective practices relevant to management, consulting, training, human resources, organizational development, corporate and nonprofit communication. Strengthens communication foundations in coordination, adaptation and problem-solving that are relevant to effectiveness in civic, professional and community organizations. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Investigates how organizational structures are created, changed and sustained through communication. Considers ways assumptions about authority, participation or efficiency may be complicated through theoretical and analytical study. Encourages recognition of communication as both a tool and a site of influence, constraint and negotiation in organizational settings. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of communication systems and networks; analysis of organizational cultures and practices of socialization; consideration of power, leadership and decision-making; exploration of conflict, collaboration and change; examination of technology, identity and structure in organizational life; attention to communication challenges that emerge in diverse or multi-level organizations. Examples or case discussions may draw from corporate, governmental, nonprofit, academic and/or community contexts.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines strategic communication through the study of how organizations plan, design and implement communication campaigns. Examines how communication strategies are developed to align stakeholder needs with organizational goals within public environments. Considers planning models, message design, effective tactics, channel selection, evaluation, budgeting and collaboration with community or client partners. Emphasizes analysis, problem-solving and adaptation of communication practices across professional, nonprofit and/or civic contexts. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Connects strategic communication to professional contexts, such as public relations, integrated marketing communication, nonprofit campaigns and initiatives, branding, media production and/or organizational communication. Develops skills and foundations relevant to situation, organization, and stakeholder analysis, campaign planning, message development, collaboration with stakeholders and applied research. Aligns with marketplace settings where communication is used to shape perception, coordinate action and address public needs or organizational challenges. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how strategic communication differs from general messaging, sales or promotion. Highlights the role of planning, research and ethics in shaping communication outcomes. Encourages reflection on how strategy must adjust to different audiences, purposes and constraints, rather than relying on a single model or platform. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include case analysis of campaigns; study of stakeholder identification, goals and messaging; application of communication research; media writing and visual communication; channel strategy; budgeting, collaboration with organizations; evaluation and adaptation of communication plans. Course projects or examples may involve nonprofit, corporate, governmental or community settings and may draw on diverse perspectives and public issues.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in COMM 323 and COMM 322; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the strategic use of communication tactics in public and organizational contexts. Focuses on writing, planning and integrating traditional and digital media tools to support communication goals. Considers research, message and design development, media platforms and message evaluation. Examines how communication tactics are shaped by audiences, objectives, timing and professional standards. Includes analysis of how digital and legacy media operate in strategic communication campaigns across profit and nonprofit sectors. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Connects strategic communication to professional contexts, such as public relations, nonprofit campaigns, branding, integrated marketing communication, media production and organizational communication. Involves skills relevant to media writing, developing and designing content for campaigns, coordinating tactics across channels and adapting messages to audiences. Aligns with marketplace expectations in sectors that use communication to engage stakeholders, manage reputation or support organizational goals. Supports preparation for advanced study in communication, media strategy or related professional fields. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies that strategic communication involves planning, research and audience understanding; not just choosing platforms or sending messages. Highlights the relationship between communication tactics, planning, persuasion, credibility and ethics. Builds awareness of how media platforms influence message design and implementation, stakeholder response and public perception. Promotes critical thinking about communication choices and their consequences in real-world contexts. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of digital and traditional media tools; development of written and visual content; research for message planning; integration of communication tactics across platforms; evaluation of effectiveness; writing for news, Associated Press Style, features, public relations writing, social media and multimedia formats; audience targeting and message tailoring; portfolio-building; and collaboration with client, community or organizational partners. Content may incorporate diverse perspectives connected to stakeholder demographics, institutional needs and/or community contexts, as relevant to strategic communication work.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in COMM 323, junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how strategic communication is used to shape policy, manage reputation and advance organizational goals across profit and nonprofit settings. Focuses on planning models, stakeholder analysis, campaign strategy and message design. Considers how communication tools are selected, adapted and evaluated in relation to audiences, goals and contexts. Examines ethical, legal and social dimensions of strategic practice. Includes study of branding, advocacy, media use and organizational communication across institutional, public and marketplace environments. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to fields such as public relations, public affairs, advocacy, corporate communication, nonprofit outreach, integrated marketing communication, branding and campaign management. Involves practices relevant to stakeholder engagement, message planning and strategic messaging across platforms. Supports preparation for professional roles that require designing, coordinating or evaluating communication strategies, as well as for advanced study in communication and related fields. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how strategic communication differs from general messaging or publicity. Highlights the role of research, planning, persuasion, ethics and stakeholder analysis in shaping outcomes. Encourages consideration of how communication strategy interacts with stakeholder behavior, power, policy and public opinion across institutional contexts. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of campaign planning, stakeholder identification, strategic messaging, branding, media selection, ethics, policy communication and/or public influence. Course content may draw on political, corporate, governmental, community, health and/or nonprofit case contexts. Examples and applications may involve public issues, institutional challenges or policy debates as relevant to strategic communication practice.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines leadership and conflict through a communication lens. Focuses on how people create shared understandings of what “counts” as leadership and how leaders manage tensions and conflicts as they seek to exert influence, coordinate collaborative efforts and mobilize collective action. Considers conflict as a communicative phenomenon in interpersonal, group, organizational and societal settings. Emphasizes how different meanings of leadership and conflict are constructed, contested and transformed through communication. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Connects to professional, organizational, civic and community contexts where leadership and conflict management are central to collaboration and decision-making. Relevant to careers involving teamwork, supervision, facilitation, advocacy, public affairs, consultation and organizational development. Addresses communication practices used to build credibility, respond to tension, coordinate diverse perspectives and guide collective problem solving. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how leadership is enacted through communication rather than position or personality. Highlights the inevitability of conflict in common leadership contexts and the range of communicative responses it can elicit. Encourages analysis of how power, relationships and context shape approaches to collaboration and disagreement. Differentiates between constructive and destructive communication patterns in navigating conflict. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of leadership theories as communication phenomena; analysis of dialogue, negotiation and mediation; examination of conflict in interpersonal, group, organizational and public settings; systemic and constructionist approaches to collaboration; use of symbols in leadership communication; management of difference in diverse teams and communities. Examples may address professional, civic, institutional and/or societal contexts in which leadership communication shapes outcomes and relationships.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Study of persuasive communication across interpersonal, group, organizational and public contexts. Examination of how messages influence beliefs, attitudes and behavior through rhetorical, psychological and social processes. Focus on audience analysis, source credibility, language, nonverbal influence, motivational appeals, ethics and theories of attitude change. Includes engagement with real-world persuasive contexts that may involve topics and examples that are politically, culturally and/or socially contested, examined for the purpose of understanding how persuasive communication operates. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applicable to communication work in media, health, politics, marketing, advocacy, leadership and organizational contexts. Informs message design, audience adaptation and analysis of influence strategies across professional and public settings. Relevant to professional fields that require reasoning, strategic communication and interpretation of persuasive efforts in civic, commercial or interpersonal life. Builds awareness of how persuasion operates in campaigns, advertising, negotiations and/or community outreach. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how persuasion involves more than argument or performance, incorporating credibility, motivation, perception, emotion and context. Distinguishes between influence, coercion, propaganda and ethical advocacy. Highlights how attitudes and judgments are shaped by message design, social norms, personal experience and situational factors. Encourages reflection on how persuasive communication functions within everyday decision-making and public discourse. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of persuasive theories; study of attitudes and attitude change; credibility and message design; emotional and motivational appeals; ethical considerations in persuasion; influence in interpersonal, group and mediated settings; language, nonverbal strategies and message framing; resistance, compliance, refutation and evaluation of persuasive claims. Course examples may involve public health messaging, political communication, advertising, advocacy campaigns and/or other areas where the use of persuasive strategies is debated or contested.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how integrated communication supports the planning and execution of events in professional, organizational and community contexts. Focus on coordination of information, people, logistics, budgets and messaging across settings such as conferences, corporate functions, nonprofit initiatives, celebrations and outreach programs. Attention to theory-informed planning (praxis), interpersonal and organizational communication processes and the role of events in shaping stakeholder relationships and public engagement. Considers how context, culture, goals, audience expectations and needs influence communication choices in event design and management. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to fields involving strategic communication, public relations, marketing, corporate communication, nonprofit outreach, hospitality, fundraising and community engagement. Informs work that involves planning, promoting and coordinating events for internal or public audiences. Relevant to careers requiring collaboration across departments, client relations, sponsorship development, logistics management and message design. Supports preparation for roles in which communication strategy, leadership, coordination and audience experience are central to outcomes. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how event planning relies on communication as both organizational practice and strategic action. Clarifies how decisions about language, symbolism, audience and presentation shape perception, participation and impact. Encourages recognition of how events reflect cultural norms, organizational identity and stakeholder expectations. Emphasizes the connection between communication theory and decision making in real-world planning environments. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of integrated communication strategy in event design; analysis of interpersonal, group and organizational coordination; consideration of budgeting, logistics, promotion and stakeholder engagement; exploration of leadership, negotiation and problem solving in planned events; application of theory-informed planning models; examination of crisis planning, evaluation and ethical or legal considerations. Content may incorporate diverse contexts and audiences, reflecting variations in purpose, culture and/or community needs.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Nontechnical study of how communication technologies shape interpersonal, group and public communication. Surveys the development and uses of media and digital platforms, including how technological change influences interaction, access and social practices. Examines the relationship between communication technologies, culture, industry and everyday life. Engagement with real-world issues and diverse perspectives may occur when examining how communication technologies intersect with politics, culture, ethics and/or lived experience. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to fields involving digital communication, media industries, advertising and public relations, advocacy, public affairs, journalism, organizational communication and technology-focused professions. Informs understanding of how communication practices adapt to emerging tools and platforms in professional, civic and community contexts. Connects to work involving media production, analysis, information sharing, digital literacy, media law and public communication across changing technological environments. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how communication is shaped not only by speakers and audiences but also by technological systems, infrastructures and access. Clarifies differences between viewing technology as a neutral tool and as a force that influences culture, power, participation and/or identity. Encourages reflection on how media shape perception, connection, persuasion and public dialogue in ways that are not always readily visible. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of communication technologies and their history; influence of technology on interpersonal, group and public communication; media industries and convergence; digital platforms and social change; argumentation and persuasion in technological debates; access, ethics and policy; cultural and societal effects of emerging media; considerations of how new and traditional media intersect in shaping information, identity and participation in contemporary society. Content may address contested or controversial issues related to technological innovation, communication practices and/or public discourse.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in COMM 230/JOUR 230.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of communication across cultural contexts, examining how meaning, identity and relationship-building are influenced by cultural norms, values and/or assumptions. Focuses on verbal and nonverbal interaction styles, language practices, adaptation and culture shock, and the role of history, power and context in shaping interpretation. Course content may draw on examples from everyday life, media, organizational settings and global encounters. Course material and discussion may reference unfamiliar or sensitive cultural perspectives for purposes of comparison and analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds practical awareness for communicating in workplaces, teams, service settings and digital environments where differences in expectations or expression may affect collaboration. Supports careers involving client communication, international coordination, education, public service or leadership by strengthening skills in perception-checking, listening and navigating ambiguity. Provides foundations for academic study in communication, cultural studies and global affairs, while supporting civic readiness and ethical intercultural engagement. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Builds recognition of how cultural background shapes assumptions. Considers how interpretations can be influenced by habit rather than intent and how misunderstandings may result from differing expectations rather than disagreement. Considers perspectives on “culture” that extend beyond nationality to include age, profession, region, gender, religion or other social frameworks that shape interaction and interpretation. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of cultural values and worldviews; verbal and nonverbal communication styles; identity negotiation and stereotyping; intercultural relationships and conflict; migration, tourism or globalization as sites of communication; media and popular culture as representations of cultural difference. Course material may include depictions of unfamiliar cultural practices or contested norms, examined to understand how communication patterns emerge across cultural differences.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Qatar campus.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of popular culture as a site of communication and meaning-making. Examines how media forms such as television, film, music, sports, fashion, games and digital platforms shape and reflect social values, identities, ideologies and/or collective experience. Surveys critical and rhetorical approaches used to analyze cultural texts, social practices, conceptual maps and media industries. Attention to how popular culture communicates meaning in everyday life and contested topics surrounding such concerns as gender, sexuality, race, class and technology. Engagement with real-world issues and diverse perspectives may arise through topics connected to politics, culture, ethics and/or lived experience. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to careers in media, communication, journalism, entertainment and content creation. Develops skills in critical interpretation, message analysis, meaning-making, media literacy and understanding impact on audiences, communities and publics. Informs work in marketing, storytelling, strategic communication and public culture. Supports engagement with cultural discourse in civic, professional and institutional settings. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how popular culture operates as ideology, expressive activities and a form of social communication. Clarifies how everyday media production, representation and consumption relate to questions of influence, identity, community and belonging. Encourages examination of familiar cultural texts with greater attention to context, meaning and interpretation. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of cultural theory and media criticism; analysis of television, music, film, sports, fashion, games and/or digital culture; exploration of representation and identity in media; consideration of politics, fandom, celebrity, persuasion, technology and leisure; examination of how popular culture shapes and responds to public discourse. Course material may include content ranging from light entertainment to content involving violence, gender, race, sexuality, religion or contested social issues as relevant to understanding communication and popular culture.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Qatar campus.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores key concepts and theories for understanding how communication both reflects and shapes diversity in today’s world. Students study the mutual constitution of culture and communication, or the idea that communication practices both shape culture and are shaped by it. Examines one or more dimensions of identity, including gender, race, ethnicity, sexuality, social class, ability, nationality and religion, and how these dimensions affect communication across personal, organizational, public and/or other contexts. Includes practice in analyzing communication through critical and cultural perspectives. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Equips students with tools to navigate communication in diverse personal, professional and civic settings. Concepts and perspectives studied here apply directly to working in multicultural teams, exercising inclusive leadership and adapting to varied audiences in workplace and public contexts. Beyond career preparation, the course fosters critical awareness of how communication practices shape social realities, offering frameworks for lifelong learning, responsible citizenship and public/community engagement. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how terms such as culture, identity and diversity are defined within communication research and scholarly traditions, which may differ from everyday usage. Demonstrates how these concepts shape interaction, expectations and interpretation, revealing contexts in which cultural difference functions as a central dimension of communicative practice. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of how communication reflects and shapes cultural difference; study of identity across dimensions such as gender, race, ethnicity, sexuality, social class, ability, nationality and/or religion; analysis of how communication practices can reinforce or challenge inequity; consideration of communication across interpersonal, organizational and/or public contexts; introduction to critical and cultural perspectives on communication and diversity. Course may include content that is controversial or contested, as relevant to examining the ways differences in belief, perspective and lived experience shape communication practices.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the structures, economics and regulation of media industries across sectors such as film, television, music, publishing, video games, streaming and/or digital platforms. Examines how content is produced, financed, distributed and governed within commercial, public and hybrid systems. Considers trends in media ownership, labor practices, media convergence, globalization, audience markets and/or media policy. Attention to the roles of technology, culture and/or law in shaping how media industries operate. Course material may engage with real-world issues involving politics, regulation, representation and/or controversy, as relevant to understanding industry practices. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to careers in media production, media law and policy, journalism, strategic communication, entertainment management, marketing, publishing and digital platforms. Informs understanding of how media businesses make decisions, respond to regulatory pressures and adapt to changing technologies and audiences. Supports advanced study in media studies, communication, business, law and policy. Useful for those navigating or analyzing industries shaped by ownership structures, market forces and cultural influence. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how media industries function beyond consumption and cultural familiarity. Highlights the interplay of economic interests, creative labor, technology and public policy. Encourages recognition of the power dynamics and institutional processes that shape media access, visibility and innovation. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of media ownership and consolidation; production, distribution and exhibition systems; financing models and supply-chain relations; regulation and public policy; labor and creative work; technology and convergence; niche and mass markets; globalization and cultural circulation; media ethics and advocacy. Examples may draw on current and historical cases across major and emerging sectors.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how media and technology represent, reinforce and challenge ideas about identity, power and social differences. Examines theories of communication and culture to understand how media shape and are shaped by beliefs about race, gender, class, sexuality, ability, nationality and/or religion. Considers how communication practices construct and contest meanings of belonging, visibility and participation. Engagement with real-world issues and diverse perspectives may involve topics that are culturally, politically and/or socially sensitive, discussed for the purpose of academic analysis and critical understanding. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Provides foundations for future professionals in journalism, digital media, strategic communication, public advocacy and related fields to anticipate audience response, avoid misrepresentation and build public trust. Builds transferable skills in media literacy, cultural analysis and ethical communication across professional and civic settings. Supports excellence in leadership and teamwork in diverse workplaces by considering how identity and difference influence communication dynamics. Supports advanced study in media studies, communication, cultural studies and related areas concerned with diversity and representation. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how cultural identities and media forms are interdependent, showing how meaning, power and visibility are negotiated through communication. Encourages reflection on the social roles of media institutions, creators and audiences in shaping public discourse and cultural imagination. Highlights the importance of dialogue, critical awareness and informed engagement in multicultural and mediated environments. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include representation and ideology in film, television, music and digital platforms; intersectionality and social identity; media and power; race, gender and sexuality in cultural production; class, globalization and inequality; disability and visibility; fandom, subcultures and participatory media; and contemporary debates around bias, equity and inclusion. Course material may include media content addressing real-world controversies or differing viewpoints, as relevant to understanding media, culture and identity.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores theoretical approaches to understanding how media shapes and is shaped by communication, perception, multiple axes of social identity and/or social behavior. Surveys models of media processes and effects, including cognitive, behavioral and sociocultural perspectives. Examines how media theory explains influence, interpretation and interaction across traditional and digital platforms. Emphasizes how theories function within social-scientific research and guide analysis of mediated experience. Discussion may include contemporary issues and/or case studies involving controversial or sensitive topics, addressed for purposes of theoretical and empirical understanding. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to careers in media research, strategic communication, journalism, digital analytics and audience engagement. Builds knowledge of how theoretical frameworks support evidence-based reasoning, message design and interpretation, and media strategy. Contributes to professional and academic preparation in fields that rely on understanding media processes, including marketing, public relations, public policy, journalism and communication science. Supports civic literacy by exploring how mediated communication might influence opinion, participation and information exchange. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how media theory connects abstract ideas with empirical study, distinguishing theoretical explanation from personal impression or political interpretation. Highlights how systematic approaches reveal the mechanisms and conditions under which media affect individuals and society. Encourages appreciation of theory as a tool for interpreting complexity, rather than prescribing belief or ideology. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of major traditions and frameworks explaining how media shape perception, thought, multiple axes of social identity and social experience; examination of theories of media effects, audience behavior and communication influence; exploration of how theory functions in research, guiding explanation, prediction and interpretation across print, broadcast, digital and networked media. Course material may address real-world examples and controversies involving technology, news, politics or entertainment, as relevant to understanding how communication theories explain mediated processes and effects.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the intersections of communication, economics and power in a global context. Focuses on how media systems, industries and platforms are shaped by political and economic forces and how communication practices in turn influence markets, policies and/or governance. Considers both historical foundations and contemporary debates, including regulation, globalization and/or digital capitalism. Attention to how communication systems distribute resources, opportunities and influence across societies. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops critical tools for analyzing media institutions, technologies and policies. Builds competence in understanding how communication systems affect civic life, professional practice and global relations. Strengthens media literacy and prepares students for roles in journalism, policymaking and organizations where knowledge of communication structures and their consequences is essential. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how communication systems are not neutral but embedded in structures of power, economics and culture. Highlights competing perspectives about surveillance, democracy, inequality and/or globalization. Highlights how theories and practices of communication differ across regions and traditions, fostering a more nuanced view of the global information society. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of media industries and markets; regulation, law and policy; globalization of communication systems; political and economic theories of media; surveillance and data economies; digital platforms and technology governance; communication and inequality; comparative perspectives from the Global North and Global South; debates over freedom, accountability and reform. Course discussion may involve contemporary cases and controversial issues, addressed for purposes of analysis and critique within an environment of respectful dialogue.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the origins and development of media systems across historical eras, from early symbolic communication to contemporary digital networks to technological platforms. Examines how media technologies, institutions and practices have shaped — and have been shaped by — political power, cultural values, social movements and/or economic forces. Considers media not only as tools of expression but as infrastructures that organize public life, regulate access to information and influence how communities govern, remember and relate. Engagement with real-world historical cases may include political conflict, cultural controversy, censorship, access and/or control, presented for purposes of scholarly analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Supports careers and advanced study in media industries, journalism, archiving or educational work. Builds understanding of how media systems evolve, why regulatory structures matter and how technological change alters public discourse, democracy, everyday life and civic participation. Provides historical perspective useful for interpreting present-day debates on platform governance, free speech, misinformation and media consolidation. Strengthens civic literacy by tracing how media systems reflect and reshape democratic values, cultural identity and public power. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies that media history is not a linear story of innovation but an ongoing struggle over access, authority and meaning. Highlights how technologies such as printing, broadcasting, telephony and internet platforms have been shaped by policy decisions, economic interests, political desires and/or cultural anxieties and not just by invention and innovation. Encourages reflection on how present-day media assumptions differ from historical practices and how contemporary systems may one day be viewed as contested rather than inevitable. TOPICS AND THEMES. Study of media origins from oral and symbolic communication to print, telegraphy, broadcasting, film and digital networks; how media system relate to state power, commerce, religion, social movements and everyday life; impacts of infrastructure and regulation, censorship and press freedom, media monopolies and public access; and recurring questions such as: Who controls communication? How do new media displace or transform older systems? When does media empower or exclude? Course material may draw on historical examples involving political dissent, propaganda, moral regulation and cultural conflict to illustrate dynamics of media change.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores key concepts, theories and practices in international communication and global journalism. Examines comparative media systems by analyzing how media develops across different political, cultural and economic contexts. Considers how world news circulates: who produces it, how it travels and how it is interpreted by diverse audiences. Examines issues such as freedom of the press, political propaganda, international advertising, public diplomacy and/or the impact of digital technologies. Students engage with theoretical, pragmatic, political and/or ethical perspectives to analyze how power, culture and/or technology shape global information exchange. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Equips students with tools for working with global media across cultural differences. Builds skills in evaluating international news, identifying propaganda and disinformation and applying ethical standards across cultures. Prepares students for careers in journalism, public affairs and related fields requiring cross-cultural awareness and media literacy. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Develops understandings of press freedom, news values and global information flows, recognizing that media systems operate within distinct political, cultural and economic contexts; exploring how interconnected stories affecting different countries and regions have developed through globalization and social media. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of comparative media systems; study of world news flows and international reporting; press freedom, censorship and ethics; political propaganda, public diplomacy and soft power; international advertising and global news cultures; impact of digital technologies, social media and generative AI; challenges of disinformation and “fake news” in global communication. Course materials may include discussion of sensitive or controversial topics, presented from multiple perspectives to reflect the diversity of global media.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; COMM-365 also taught at Qatar campus.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores theories, research and practices of health communication across interpersonal, organizational, cultural and/or mediated contexts. Focuses on how communication shapes health beliefs, behaviors and outcomes in clinical, community and/or policy settings. Considers patient-provider interaction, communication in health care organizations, health campaigns, media representations of health and/or cultural perspectives on illness and well-being. Attention to the role of technology and social media in shaping health communication environments. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds competence in applying communication strategies to health-related issues across professional, civic and personal life. Strengthens skills relevant to health professions, study of advocacy, policy and media. Develops awareness of how communication influences health literacy, patient outcomes and public understanding of health. Prepares for advanced study for roles in organizations and industries where health communication is central. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday views of health and illness differ from those developed through research and cultural analysis. Studies ways health communication involves not only the exchange of information but also negotiation of meaning, culture and/or power. Considers how communication practices influence perceptions of wellness, treatment and/or health equity. Course may involve engagement with sensitive topics such as illness, mortality, mental health, reproductive health and public health controversies. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of patient-provider communication, organizational communication in health care systems and communication in health policy and study of advocacy; exploration of health campaigns, media representations and the use of technology and social media in promoting health; consideration of social support, cultural perspectives on health and illness and the role of communication in shaping individual and collective health outcomes. Topics may also involve contested or sensitive issues, including health disparities, reproductive health, addiction, mental health and/or public health campaigns, examined for their communicative and cultural significance.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of media audiences across empirical and interpretive research traditions. Examines how audiences are measured, targeted, persuaded, entertained and/or mobilized in effects-based frameworks. Considers how audiences might interpret, resist or rework media. Explores audience engagement with such content as news, entertainment, political communication, health messaging and advertising. Addresses how age, identity, ideology and/or context shape audience reception and response. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages practices central to media strategy, public communication, digital analytics, outreach and message design. Builds understanding of how audiences are researched, segmented and addressed in journalism, advertising, public health, politics, entertainment and digital media industries. Supports academic preparation in media effects theory, reception theory and communication research. Enhances awareness of how audience behavior shapes public discourse. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Complicates everyday assumptions that audiences passively receive media or predictably react to it. Highlights how persuasion and interpretation emerge through interaction between media content, audience predispositions and/or social contexts. Emphasizes that the study of mass media audiences requires attention to both influence and agency, data, and context. TOPICS AND THEMES. Study of audience behavior across news, entertainment, advertising and/or digital platforms; examination of media effects models, interpretive reception theories and audience participation logics; analysis of how audiences attend, interpret, resist or repurpose media content; consideration of political messaging, health campaigns, consumer persuasion, fandom and/or public controversy as sites for audience analysis. Examples may include media involving politics, public health, identity or moral debate when relevant to understanding media audiences. Course material may reference real-world cases or contested media environments for the purpose of analysis.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how communication functions as a strategic resource in entrepreneurial environments shaped by digital media. Examines how ventures mobilize economic, social, cultural and/or symbolic capital through branding, networking, design and storytelling. Introduces foundational theories of free market entrepreneurship culture to analyze how new media can affect barriers to entry and existing inequalities. Considers entrepreneurship as a communicative process of positioning, persuasion, collaboration and identity-building. Course projects involve developing mock enterprises that utilize multiple aspects of digital marketing, such as social media, photography, videography and web design. Course material may include discussion of prominent entrepreneurs, companies, disruptive technologies, strategic foresight and/or contested business practices. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Enhances entrepreneurial insight with practical communication strategies, demonstrating how the same media practices apply in both startup initiatives and established organizational environments. Builds marketable competencies in branding, messaging, audience analysis, collaboration and digital production, which are relevant to careers in marketing, public communication, content development, nonprofit advocacy and independent media ventures. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in communication, media studies, business, design or innovation fields. Strengthens professional and career preparation by illuminating how digital platforms structure access, influence and/or participation in public discourse. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies entrepreneurial models and highlights the interplay between economic opportunity and cultural participation. Examines how entrepreneurial success relies on the interplay between social networks, design decisions and public perception as much as financial capital. Illuminates collaborative entrepreneurial possibilities and clarifies how digital visibility can democratize as well as reinforce hierarchy. Considers how entrepreneurial narratives, whether inspirational or cautionary, can reflect broader assumptions about risk, merit, innovation and/or matters of equality. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of branding and identity-building across digital platforms; analysis of audience engagement strategies, crowdfunding models and influencer economies; exploration of social capital, cultural capital and symbolic capital as resources in entrepreneurial communication; consideration of collaborative media production and co-creation practices. Course material may reference past real-world ventures, ranging from grassroots movements to commercial startups, including examples involving economic disparity, controversial branding and/or public media backlash.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in COMM 275/JOUR 275 or JOUR 275/COMM 275; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how gender, race, sexuality, ethnicity and related identities are produced, represented, negotiated, contested, consumed and/or performed in relation to media. Explores contributions of historically marginalized groups to media production, alongside analysis of how these groups have been portrayed as characters, audiences, communities and/or target markets. Focuses on media as a site of competing commercial, cultural, political, satirical and/or resistance narratives, rather than as a single, unified voice. Emphasizes critical interpretation of media texts and systems, while allowing space for multiple viewpoints and interpretations. Course material may include historical and contemporary examples that reflect both progress and controversy, analyzed for their cultural and communicative significance. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages issues central to media literacy, political economy, representation and audience awareness in contemporary communication industries. Builds recognition of the ways portrayals of gender and race shape perception, credibility and/or trust in journalism, entertainment, advertising, representatives, community and public communication. Supports careers in communication, media industries, public relations, education, nonprofit work and leadership roles where navigating diverse audiences is essential. Supports informed decision-making in professional and civic contexts by highlighting how media representations influence identity, inclusion and public dialogue. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies that studying media portrayals of gender and race is not limited to celebration or criticism but involves examining how representation functions within broader cultural, social, economic, political and/or institutional systems. Illustrates how media are grounded in economies of production, representation and consumption across platforms, products and pipelines. Considers ways media might be empowering, stereotypical, commercial and/or transformative, depending on context, audience and community. Promotes awareness that interpretations of media content may differ across social, cultural and/or generational perspectives and that disagreement over meaning is part of scholarly analysis rather than a flaw in the material. Normalizes engagement with sensitive or contested topics as a means of understanding how media both reflect and shape public life. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of media across film, television, news, advertising, music and digital platforms through production, representation and consumption; analysis of gender, race, ethnicity and intersectional identities in historical and contemporary contexts; consideration of media production practices, audience reception and the economic and institutional forces shaping representation; examination of stereotypes, invisibility, empowerment narratives and commercialized identity; discussion of how media both reinforce and challenge social norms related to power, privilege and belonging. Course material may include content that reflects real-world disparities or conflicting viewpoints.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines popular music as a form of communication shaped by technology, industry structures and cultural context. Traces how radio broadcasting, recording formats and digital platforms influence music creation, distribution and listening practices. Considers music as both entertainment and public discourse, attending to how artists, audiences and institutions construct meaning through sound, performance and/or media presence. Engagement with music connected to politics, commerce, identity or ethics may occur for the purpose of understanding communication processes. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Strengthens the ability to recognize how audio is used in journalism, marketing and civic communication to guide emotion and interpretation. Supports preparation for careers in media industries, music journalism, broadcasting, content strategy, audience analysis and arts promotion. Enhances critical and professional awareness of how music circulates in commercial and public life, informing work in creative industries, cultural analysis and public communication. Provides academic grounding for advanced study in media, culture, communication or popular music studies. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies distinctions between personal taste and scholarly analysis of music as communication. Encourages recognition of how technological formats, business models and cultural narratives influence what becomes popular, forgotten and/or controversial. Highlights both celebratory and critical perspectives on musical innovation, nostalgia and/or appropriation. Offers historical and structural context to familiar sounds, revealing music as shaped as much by systems as by creativity. TOPICS AND THEMES. Study of radio broadcasting, record production and digital platform economies; analysis of genre formation and evolution; examination of music as storytelling, identity performance or political expression; exploration of fan cultures, nostalgia, authenticity and commercialization; consideration of how sound, image, celebrity and community intersect in shaping perception. Instructional approaches may emphasize historical development, media industries, genre evolution and/or identity and representation within musical cultures.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of motherhood as a cultural, social and communicative construct rather than a singular biological or personal identity. Examines how ideas about motherhood are created, reinforced or challenged through literature, film, popular media, digital media, political rhetoric, public policy, advertising, news, medical institutions and/or everyday discourse across different time periods and cultural contexts. Considers both idealized and marginalized portrayals, attending to such matters as gender, race, class, sexuality, ability and nation. Course material may include historical texts, contemporary examples, commentary and/or fictional representations. Content may include portrayals that are celebratory, critical or controversial, examined for purposes of interpretation. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds critical literacy for analyzing how cultural expectations shape perceptions of family, caregiving and social roles. Promotes awareness of how media narratives, cultural practices and public discourse influence policies, workplace norms, interpersonal expectations and public debates surrounding parenting, labor and care work. Supports workforce preparation in fields such as media, healthcare, public health, social work, policy development, education and public communication where sensitivity to diverse family structures and practices is essential. Enhances academic readiness for further study in rhetoric, gender studies, media studies and/or cultural studies. Encourages reflection on how public narratives about motherhood have evolved over time, affect social inclusion, policy decisions and public life. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how ideas about motherhood vary across cultures, eras, socio-economic groups and/or ideological perspectives, challenging assumptions of universality. Encourages recognition of both biological and socially constructed dimensions of maternal identity. Clarifies the difference between personal belief and cultural representation, prompting reflection on how individuals internalize or resist public narratives about care, responsibility and motherhood and how it may modify behavior. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of motherhood in literature, film, television, music, news, advertising, music and digital media; historical shifts in maternal ideals; feminist and anti-feminist discourses; motherhood and labor; political uses of maternal identity; race, class and marginalized motherhoods; disability and motherhood; reproductive technology and infertility narratives; representation of motherhood in children's literature and films, childfree identities and resistance to maternal norms. Course material may involve emotional and sensitive content such as depictions of grief, trauma, marginalization or public controversy as relevant to understanding how motherhood is framed in culture.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how new media technologies shape civic participation, public discourse and/or social change across different political systems. Focus on communication practices in democratic, authoritarian and/or transitional societies. Considers how digital platforms enable organizing, surveillance, protest and/or community formation. Emphasizes theory-driven analysis of how online communication intersects with power, governance and collective life. Engagement with case studies from global and/or local contexts, including instances where media use is celebrated, contested or restricted. Course content and discussions may draw from different cultural or political contexts, including situations of disagreement or unrest, examined for purposes of understanding communication dynamics. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Emphasizes the role of digital communication in public affairs, advocacy, crisis response and institutional communication. Builds awareness of how media strategies function in political campaigns, nonprofit initiatives, international development and grassroots organizations. Supports professional work in public communication, policy analysis, journalism, technology sectors and civic engagement. Provides academic grounding for advanced study in media, politics, globalization or communication. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Complicates everyday assumptions about social media as inherently liberating or harmful. Encourages nuanced understanding of how digital tools can empower expression while reinforcing inequality or control. Highlights tensions between visibility and vulnerability, participation and manipulation. Models disagreement and controversy as part of understanding communication in public life rather than advocacy for a particular stance. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of civic participation and digital public spheres; analysis of social media activism, political protest and networked movements; examination of platform governance, censorship, surveillance and state messaging; consideration of misinformation, polarization, digital propaganda and extremist communication; exploration of online community-building, identity expression and digital inequalities; comparative perspectives across democratic, authoritarian and transitional societies. Course material may reference real-world cases involving political or cultural controversy, including but not limited to violence, hate speech or ideological conflict, for purposes of understanding how new media intersects with civic life, governance and social dynamics.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of how gender shapes and is shaped by communication across interpersonal, organizational and public contexts. Examines how people express, interpret and negotiate gender in everyday interaction, media environments and/or institutional settings. Explores both stability and change in gendered expectations, roles and identities. Course content and discussions may touch on differing perspectives or points of disagreement for purposes of understanding communication dynamics surrounding gender. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Supports career pathways in media, public service, advocacy, education, law, nonprofit work and other community-facing professions by examining communication as grounded in diverse communities and lived experiences. Enhances preparation for careers involving interpersonal interaction, public communication, education, health, social work, policy development, human relations, consulting, advocacy or management. Builds recognition of how communication norms vary across individuals, cultures and contexts, which is an essential competency for workplace effectiveness, civic participation and collaborative problem-solving. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Explores how communication research addresses biological sex alongside cultural understandings of gender identity and gender roles and how each may influence interaction across different contexts. Highlights that everyday assumptions about gender and communication can vary across individuals, cultures and/or historical periods. Encourages examination of multiple scholarly perspectives on how gender-related patterns emerge, are perceived or are reinforced through communication, without prescribing a single interpretive lens. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of gendered language, voice and nonverbal expression; feminist and critical perspectives on communication and gender; communication across friendship, romantic, family and workplace relationships; leadership, authority and collaboration in professional settings; media portrayals of femininity, masculinity and gender diversity; intersections of gender with race, sexuality, class, nationality, religion and/or ability; communication surrounding health, body image, caregiving or identity disclosure; historical and cross-cultural perspectives on gender roles and expectations; analysis of humor, conflict, persuasion or storytelling through a gendered lens. Course material may reference real-world cases involving disagreement or controversy as relevant to understanding communication dynamics.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how ideas about Latino identity and community, referred to collectively as Latinidad, are shaped through communication in public, institutional and/or interpersonal settings. Considers how people of Latin American heritage are represented in media, politics and everyday discourse, as well as how they speak, advocate and organize on their own terms. Addresses how language, history and cultural references are used to signal belonging, draw boundaries and/or negotiate differences. Course content and discussion may engage topics related to nationality, race, gender, migration and/or public controversy for purposes of analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Supports career pathways in media, public service, advocacy, education, law, nonprofit work and other community-facing professions by examining communication processes grounded in communities and lived experiences. Develops competencies for workplace effectiveness, civic participation and collaborative problem-solving by building recognition of how communication norms can vary across individuals, cultures and contexts. Supports academic preparation in rhetoric, media studies, U.S. Latino studies and social research. Strengthens cultural insight critical for leadership and collaboration in multilingual or multicultural environments. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Expands recognition of Latinidad as varied rather than monolithic, shaped by history, region, generation, class, race and political context. Clarifies how categories such as “Hispanic,” “Latino/a” or “Latinx” emerge, shift and are debated over time. Highlights how communication both reflects and challenges social hierarchies, encouraging reflection on how voices are amplified, stereotyped or overlooked across public life. Frames identity as negotiated and relational, not assumed or imposed. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of Latino social movements and protest rhetoric; institutional and governmental discourse about immigration or citizenship; representations of Latinidad in news, entertainment or advertising; analysis of terminology and labeling practices; narratives of space, border, diaspora or belonging; exploration of gender, race, indigeneity, class, sexuality, religion and/or Afro-Latinx identity within Latina/o/x communication. Course material may reference politically or culturally sensitive topics when relevant to understanding communication processes, approached within an environment of scholarly inquiry and respectful dialogue.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how Black freedom has been expressed across art, speech, political action, media, visual cultures and writings designed to challenge injustice, build solidarity and imagine alternative futures. Considers both well-known and lesser-known figures, recognizing that activism operates through leaders, communities and collective voices. Course content may include material involving racial conflict, oppression and struggle in the United States and/or around the globe. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds recognition of communication as a tool for social response, institutional critique and public engagement. Provides perspective for professional fields that require cultural awareness, ethical judgment and responsiveness to diverse audiences, such as education, media, public service, community leadership, law and advocacy-related work. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in rhetoric, media, history, social movements or communication. Contributes to civic understanding by tracing how ideas become actions through communication practices. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how articulations of Black freedom have long served as catalysts for action, social change and public debate in the United States and across the globe. Positions their strategies, not only as expressions of a specific community, but as case studies in persuasion, resistance, leadership and/or collective voice that have shaped constitutional interpretation, civic participation and public opinion more broadly. Considers how struggles for justice by one group reveal broader questions shared across groups, such as rights, authority, belonging and national identity. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of abolitionist writings, protest speeches, spirituals and freedom songs; rhetorical strategies of civil rights, Black Power and/or contemporary justice movements; analysis of communication through sermons, manifestos, poetry, performance and/or media; exploration of visual and digital media as tools of resistance and community-building; consideration of leadership, collective action and messaging in local and/or global liberation struggles. Course material may reference conflict, repression or political controversy as relevant to understanding communication within movements for freedom and justice. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. Instructors who teach this class may assign different readings and/or course topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how social movements communicate their goals, identities and demands through speech, writing, media and/or performance. Analyzes rhetorical strategies used to mobilize supporters, challenge and create institutions and/or shape public perception in democratic and non-democratic contexts. Highlights how meaning, legitimacy and resistance are constructed through communication across different eras. Course content and discussion may reference contentious or opposing viewpoints for the purpose of understanding persuasive practice across specific topics. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds workforce preparation for careers involving advocacy, public communication, journalism, policy, law, nonprofit work or civic leadership; building understanding of how strategic messaging, storytelling and symbolism operate in public life. Enhances ability to gauge public sentiment, assess persuasive appeals and navigate disagreement in professional and community environments. Provides academic grounding for advanced study in rhetoric, media, political communication or social change. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how definitions of “legitimate” protest or persuasion shift over time and across audiences. Considers why some tactics are celebrated while others are condemned and how public judgment is shaped by rhetoric, media coverage and institutional response. Considers social movements in terms of communication processes rather than moral binaries, revealing how communication strategies function across differing and at times opposing perspectives. TOPICS AND THEMES. Includes the study of how different groups across American history have advocated for or resisted changing the status quo. May include study of abolition, labor, suffrage, civil rights, feminist, Latina/o/x, Indigenous, environmental, gender justice, sexual rights, animal rights, student, anti-war, anti-racist, religious, conservative or populist social movements. Analysis of manifestos, speeches, protests, songs, visual rhetoric, digital campaigns or counter-movements. Exploration of strategies such as coalition-building, confrontation, satire, spectacle or moral appeal; consideration of state and media response to dissent, including repression, co-optation or commemoration. Course material may reference real-world cases involving social conflict or political controversy, examined analytically within an environment of respectful dialogue.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores rhetorical theory as a tool for analyzing persuasion, discourse and symbolic action across varied contexts. Considers how different theoretical frameworks clarify how language, images or performance influence belief, identity and/or judgment. Emphasizes application of theory to real-world communicative problems rather than abstract debate alone. Topics vary by instructor and may center on specific genres, intellectual traditions and/or individual theorists. Course content may involve materials ranging from public speeches to digital memes or popular media, examined for interpretive purposes rather than endorsement. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages communication practices relevant to leadership, advocacy, media analysis and civic or organizational strategy. Builds capacity to interpret persuasive discourse, assess rhetorical intent and/or articulate the assumptions embedded in public messages. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in rhetoric, media studies or communication theory. Contributes to professional roles that require message evaluation, argument framing or cultural awareness. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how rhetorical theory offers multiple lenses for interpreting the same message, highlighting ways meaning can be shaped by perspective rather than being fixed. Reveals how ethics, humor, philosophy, satire, activism and political discourse can operate as rhetorical strategies rather than solely as abstract ideas, entertainment or expressions of opinion. Allows engagement with unfamiliar or conflicting viewpoints as part of scholarly interpretation rather than persuasion. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of rhetorical problems such as nationalism, citizenship, identity or cultural critique; application of theories from classical, modern or contemporary traditions; examination of rhetoric as symbolic action in political, social, institutional or aesthetic contexts; exploration of discourse across spoken, written, visual or digital forms; analysis of how persuasion operates through appeals to truth, morality, identity, ritual or ideology. Specific course focus may vary by instructor, but all versions maintain emphasis on theory-driven inquiry.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores television and film as persuasive and symbolic communication. Examines rhetorical approaches to screen media, examining how narrative, genre, style, performance and/or visual form shape cultural meaning. Emphasizes close reading and critical interpretation of selected films, series and/or audiovisual texts. Course material may include popular, historical and/or controversial media — both domestic and international — analyzed for purposes of understanding communication strategy and effect. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops analytical and writing skills applicable to careers in media criticism, strategic communication, entertainment, journalism, advertising and social media. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in rhetoric, media studies, cultural analysis or related fields. Enhances civic awareness by strengthening the ability to assess how visual media influence identity, public opinion and debate. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how familiar entertainment texts function as arguments about identity, power, values or social norms. Reveals how meaning can emerge not only from content but also from framing, characterization and genre convention. Considers how television and film can provide evidence of changing cultural assumptions and act as resources for public imagination. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of genre and narrative structure; visual style and symbolism; representation of identity, morality or ideology; satire, parody and social commentary; industrial or historical context shaping production and reception; rhetorical frameworks drawn from classical, modern or contemporary theory. Course material may include programming or films involving violence, sexuality, religion and/or politically sensitive content, addressed for purposes of analysis within a respectful learning environment.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of images as forms of communication across public, cultural and institutional contexts. Examines how visuals convey meaning, evoke emotion, construct identity and/or shape public perception. Considers photography, advertising, memorials, protest imagery, comics and/or other visual texts as rhetorical and symbolic acts. Course content and discussion may include real-world imagery that reflects social conflict, violence, inequality and/or sensitive subjects for purposes of analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages visual literacy central to media work, journalism, advocacy, design and public communication. Builds recognition of how images influence opinion, memory and behavior across digital, institutional and interpersonal environments. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in media studies, rhetoric, journalism and cultural communication. Provides tools useful in professions requiring visual strategy, branding, storytelling or critical evaluation of mediated content. Contributes to civic awareness in a society where public debate increasingly occurs through images. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers ways visuals act not as neutral reflections of reality, but as constructed representations shaped by framing, selection and context. Highlights how different audiences interpret the same image differently, prompting reflection on perspective, bias and cultural positioning. Encourages recognition of how images communicate power, belonging and/or exclusion; sometimes subtly, sometimes provocatively. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of photography and public memory; advertising and consumer imagery; visual culture in politics, protest and activism; comics and graphic narrative; memorials and commemorative design; digital imagery, memes and viral circulation; depictions of identity, embodiment or community through visual media. May involve visual curation or creation of original materials. Course content may include powerful or controversial imagery, such as depictions of violence, tragedy, ideological symbolism or material some may consider profane or objectionable, examined for the purpose of informed and critical interpretation of visual communication.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines propaganda as a strategic form of communication used across political, commercial and social contexts. Surveys historical and contemporary approaches to influencing mass audiences through language, imagery, narrative and emotion. Analyzes how persuasive appeals operate in mass media, digital platforms, public relations, advertising and/or institutional messaging. Considers distinctions between information, persuasion and manipulation, with attention to credibility, transparency and ethics. Content may include real-world messages that involve political conflict, sensitive beliefs or provocative imagery, studied for purposes of critical evaluation. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds analytical tools relevant to media literacy, strategic communication, journalism, marketing, political communication and public affairs. Supports preparation for roles requiring evaluation of persuasive messaging, audience response or ethical communication practices. Enhances readiness for advanced academic study in rhetoric, media studies or communication theory. Develops civic awareness by examining how influence can operate in democratic and non-democratic environments. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how propaganda differs from persuasion; critically engaging assumptions that it is always visible, extreme or partisan. Reveals how influence can work subtly through repetition, normalization and/or emotional framing. Considers how individuals evaluate messages, assign credibility and participate in communication systems, whether intentionally or unconsciously. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of propaganda techniques in politics, advertising, public relations and entertainment; analysis of historical and contemporary campaigns; exploration of visual, verbal and digital persuasion strategies; comparison of state, commercial and grassroots messaging; examination of credibility, emotion, repetition, symbolism and narrative in persuasive appeals. Course material may reference real-world examples involving political conflict, wartime messaging, extremist rhetoric or provocative imagery that is characteristic of contemporary propaganda and necessary for understanding its full range of expression in competitive and contentious public spheres.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.
