description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Study of political communication as a central feature of democratic life. Examines how political messages are created and circulated across campaigns, institutions, movements, journalism and/or digital platforms. Focuses on how communication informs, persuades, mobilizes and/or divides public audiences, with attention to both effective strategy and ethical responsibility. Focuses on the role of political communication in shaping American political history. Course content may reference real-world political conflict, campaign rhetoric and controversial messaging strategies, examined for purposes of analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds civic literacy by strengthening the ability to recognize persuasive tactics, evaluate competing claims and interpret political messaging across media. Supports professional preparation for careers in public service, journalism, legal advocacy, strategic communication and civic leadership. Supports the ability for informed participation in elections, policy discussions or public dialogue. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how political discourse is shaped not only by logic and evidence but also by strategic goals, narrative, emotion, symbolism and framing. Explores how disagreement can function productively when guided by shared norms of deliberation, debate and mutual recognition. Develops awareness of how communication practices can either escalate division or foster understanding across political perspectives. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of campaign speeches, debates, advertisements and digital outreach; analysis of press and government relations, political journalism and media framing; exploration of grassroots mobilization, social movements and advocacy; comparison of institutional messaging across branches of government. Course material may engage contemporary political controversies or sharply divided viewpoints, addressed for purposes of understanding how communication shapes public judgment and democratic engagement.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Study of how communication practices shape the development, escalation and resolution of conflict across interpersonal, intergroup, organizational, family and/or public settings. Examines both theoretical frameworks and practical approaches to negotiation, mediation and/or facilitated dialogue. Course content may reference real-world disputes involving sensitive or emotionally charged situations, analyzed for communication insight. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds capacity for managing disagreement in personal, professional and civic environments. Strengthens competencies relevant to leadership, teamwork, client relations, human resources, counseling, public service and community engagement. Supports the ability to navigate high-stakes conversations, advocate constructively and participate effectively in decision-making processes. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers ways conflict is not always or necessarily destructive but also a potential site for clarification, innovation and relational growth. Explores how disagreement can surface unmet needs, reveal assumptions or prompt creative problem-solving when approached with strategic communication. Considers that managing conflict effectively requires awareness of both one’s own communicative choices and broader dynamics that shape interaction. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of interpersonal disputes; intergroup tensions and prejudices; workplace and organizational conflict; group decision-making dynamics; negotiation tactics and persuasive framing; mediation and third-party intervention; cultural and gender influences on conflict style; conflict in digital or mediated environments; reconciliation, apology and forgiveness. Case material may draw from personal, professional, civic or community contexts where disagreement plays a central role.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how organizations communicate with — and are shaped by — the societies in which they operate. Considers communication as a means of building organizational identity, reputation and/or legitimacy among stakeholders such as employees, customers, communities, governments and advocacy groups. Addresses how organizational messaging is used to maintain trust, manage expectations and respond to public concerns or criticism. Course content and discussion may draw on real-world cases involving corporate responsibility, crisis communication, ethics or public controversy for purposes of analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops workforce-relevant understanding of how organizations maintain credibility, manage public expectations and communicate across diverse stakeholders, including clients, employees, communities and regulators. Builds practical insight into how communication strategies influence trust, cooperation and decision-making in professional settings. Supports the ability to interpret, evaluate and respond to organizational messaging in ways that inform decision-making in both professional and civic settings. Supports academic advancement in communication studies, organizational leadership and related fields. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how organizations can relate to broader publics rather than act as isolated entities. Explores how communication choices can shape public perception, accountability and long-term viability. Considers the role of transparency/honesty, responsibility, empathy and ethical reasoning in navigating public expectations and competing interests. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of organizational identity and image; stakeholder communication and engagement; reputation management; ethics and corporate responsibility; crisis response and public accountability; communication across internal and external audiences; globalization and cultural expectations; digital communication and public scrutiny. Course material may involve discussion of reputational disputes, social or environmental issues or critiques of corporate behavior, examined for purposes of understanding organizational communication processes.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Study of communication processes that enable or hinder collaboration in dyads, teams and group settings. Considers on how dialogue, facilitation, leadership and group dynamics shape collective decision-making and problem-solving. Course activities may include applied or project-based facilitation scenarios where communication strategies are tested in practice. Course content and discussions may address issues of disagreement or public concern for purposes of understanding communication dynamics. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds workforce-ready skills in teamwork, listening, meeting facilitation, conflict navigation and collaborative problem-solving; competencies relevant in organizational, nonprofit, community and civic environments. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in organizational communication, leadership or deliberative democracy. Reinforces civic readiness by modeling constructive engagement across differing viewpoints and interests. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how group collaboration is not merely a matter of goodwill but a communicative process that can involve power, emotion, structure and shared responsibility. Explores ways that conflict and disagreement, when managed effectively, can generate innovation, trust and shared ownership rather than division. Considers leadership as a distributed and communicative practice rather than a top-down role. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of collaboration and facilitation methods; dialogue and deliberation frameworks; leadership and followership in groups; conflict management and negotiation; roles, norms and group climate; ethics of neutrality and mediator responsibility; decision-making models; communication in diverse or high-stakes teams; online versus face-to-face collaboration. Course material may draw on real-world cases or simulations involving disagreement or public issues, analyzed for communicative strategy.
prerequisites: COMM 210; junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Study of the principles and processes behind designing media campaigns across domains such as health, politics, human rights, advertising and/or the environment. Considers theory-driven planning, persuasive strategy, message execution and evaluation in mass and digital media contexts. Includes critical analysis of real-world campaign cases past and present alongside applied exercises in campaign design. Course content may feature campaign messages involving sensitive or controversial topics, examined to understand communication strategy. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds professional competencies relevant to advertising, strategic communication, public relations, health promotion, political advocacy and nonprofit outreach. Develops skills in message targeting, audience analysis, media planning and persuasive evaluation necessary for roles involving campaign development or consultancy. Supports preparation for advanced coursework in communication strategy and reinforces civic literacy by enhancing the ability to interpret and assess persuasive messaging encountered in public life. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how effective campaign messaging requires more than creativity, demanding ethical reasoning, audience insight, emotional appeal and theoretical grounding. Expands understanding of how persuasive appeals can operate differently across issues and identities, encouraging reflection on both intended and unintended effects. Frames media campaigns not only as tools for influence but also as cultural artifacts that reveal public priorities, fears and beliefs. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of campaign theory and history; message design and persuasive appeals; audience segmentation and targeting; media channel strategy across television, radio, print and digital platforms; evaluation of campaign effectiveness; social marketing and public health initiatives; political and issue advocacy; environmental and safety campaigns; crisis communication and public service announcements. Examples may draw from domestic and international cases and include campaign content that is emotional, graphic and/or politically charged, used for promoting informed, critical analysis.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how communication technologies shape and are shaped by culture, power and everyday life. Examines theories of technological change, media history and/or digital culture, including how new and emerging technologies are often met with complex social dilemmas. Draws on historical and contemporary examples to show how technologies such as telegraphy, television, social media and surveillance platforms carry assumptions about progress, identity, work and/or control. Course content may include cases involving political conflict, privacy concerns or online controversy, examined for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Supports professional preparation in fields concerned with media policy, strategic communication, digital storytelling, user experience, ethics or advocacy. Strengthens civic literacy by analyzing how technological narratives influence public trust, participation and responsibility. Builds awareness of how institutions, governments and communities negotiate access, autonomy and accountability in digital environments. Clarifies how contemporary debates over technology shape journalism, marketing, policy development, design practice and workplace communication. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals ways technology is not always neutral but can be embedded within cultural expectations, economic systems and political values. Differentiates between everyday assumptions about innovation and scholarly approaches that analyze who benefits, who is excluded and how technological systems reinforce or redistribute power. Informs reflection on how personal devices, platforms and infrastructures can shape interaction, memory, identity and/or agency. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of technological determinism and cultural shaping of technology; utopian and dystopian narratives in media; infrastructures of communication throughout history; surveillance, data tracking and privacy; identity formation in digital communities; automation, labor and human-machine relations; digital inequality and access; governance of communication technologies in democratic and non-democratic contexts. Course materials may include historical case studies or contemporary examples involving censorship, exploitation and/or graphic or profane content as relevant to understanding communication and technology.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores video games as a field of communication study, examining their development as media industries, cultural practices and technological environments. Surveys scholarship on game studies history, video game production models, audience experiences and/or game design strategies. Investigates how gameplay involves storytelling, emotion, identity and interaction across different genres and mediums. Course material may include video games or related media that contain violence, mature content or controversial themes, examined for purposes of critical analysis and informed perspectives. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages skills applicable to media strategy, entertainment industries, marketing, game design, journalism and audience analysis. Builds familiarity with economic models, platform ecosystems and/or emerging markets surrounding digital entertainment. Supports academic preparation in communication, media studies, cultural studies and technology research. Enhances civic and cultural awareness by examining how interactive media shape norms, values and public debate. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how video games function not only as entertainment but also as sites of persuasion, identity performance, experimentation and cultural meaning. Examines distinctions between technological innovation and social consequences. Informs reflection on assumptions about players, genres, violence and/or interactivity by contrasting public debates with empirical and critical research. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of game history and platform evolution; analysis of development pipelines, publishing models and global industry structures; exploration of narrative design and emotional engagement; consideration of online communities, fandoms and participatory cultures; examination of regulation, monetization, labor, access and ethics. Course material may draw from games or case studies involving conflict, gender representation or political controversy as relevant to communication analysis.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how globalization and media are intertwined across national, transnational and diasporic circuits. Explores frameworks for understanding globalization through media ownership, migration, representation, content flow, technology, everyday life and/or political influence. Considers how news, entertainment, advertising and/or digital platforms travel across regions and are reshaped by local and transnational values, communities and regulations. Highlights both integration and inequality in global media landscapes. Course content may reference political or cultural controversies, including propaganda, censorship, immigration or conflict reporting, for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds awareness of how media industries function in global markets, supporting preparation for careers in journalism, strategic communication, public affairs, media production, policy analysis and international business. Supports adaptability within multicultural and internationally connected workplaces. Develops abilities to assess media influence across national and cultural boundaries, relevant skills in organizations operating in global or multicultural environments. Strengthens academic grounding for advanced study in communication, media studies, international relations or cultural analysis. Supports civic literacy by clarifying how global media shape public opinion, diplomacy and perception between nations. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals that media are not neutral carriers of information but products of political, economic, ideological and cultural systems. Highlights how similar content can carry different meanings depending on context, history, ideology and/or regulation. Encourages reflection on how local and/or personal media environments are shaped by assumptions and practices that may differ substantially across national and cultural boundaries, fostering greater awareness of perspective and context. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of transnational media ownership and conglomerates; global circulation of news, entertainment and advertising; audiences and consumers; comparative media systems in democratic, authoritarian and transitional societies; localization and cultural adaptation; media policy, censorship and regulatory control; streaming platforms, social media and telecommunications infrastructure; migration, diaspora, citizenship and identity across borders. Course material may reference real-world cases involving political or cultural controversy, such as extremism, disinformation or state propaganda, for purposes of analysis and critique within an environment of respectful dialogue.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of how communication practices construct, contest, circulate and/or suppress contemporary issues. Focus may draw on rhetorical, critical, interpretive and/or empirical approaches to message design, media representation, public discourse and/or everyday interaction. Emphasizes analytical reading and case analysis grounded in scholarship. Course focus varies by instructor and term. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Uses the study of individual contemporary issues as a laboratory for understanding how communication shapes public problems across domains. Builds recognition of how messages influence perception, policy and action in government, health, technology, culture and/or everyday life. Develops skills relevant to professional roles involving analysis, advocacy, media interpretation, strategic messaging or organizational decision-making. Strengthens academic preparation by deepening proficiency in applying theory to real-world cases. Supports civic readiness by refining the ability to interpret competing claims, identify persuasive strategies and critically engage issues with clarity. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of how communication shapes issues related to health, environment, technology, labor, education, identity or public policy. May examine political rhetoric, media representation, scientific controversy, organizational messaging, global and transnational issues, colonialism and decoloniality and/or grassroots advocacy. Cases may draw from news, social media, institutional reports, cultural texts and/or lived experiences. Course material may include perspectives that conflict or critique one another, addressed for the purpose of understanding how issues are framed, debated and acted upon.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how communication functions across health care settings, including interpersonal interactions, organizational systems and/or public messaging. Explores approaches to patient-provider dialogue, teamwork and/or institutional communication, alongside principles used in health campaigns and information dissemination. Addresses how communication practices influence access, understanding, decision-making and/or coordination. Course material may involve discussion of sensitive health topics, addressed for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages communication practices applicable to professional effectiveness in clinical, nonprofit, corporate and public-facing health roles. Develops analytical tools for evaluating message strategies, assessing interactional dynamics and interpreting communication within institutional structures. Supports preparation for advanced study in fields related to health, communication or organizational practice, as well as for participation in public discourse surrounding health issues. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how communication in health care involves more than information delivery, incorporating factors such as context, perception, institutional procedures and interpersonal dynamics. Informs understanding of how misunderstandings emerge and ways different approaches to communication may facilitate or impede clarity, coordination and trust. Considers communication as a process with measurable effects. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of physician-patient interaction; health literacy and information accessibility; teamwork and coordination in clinical settings; communication breakdowns and system-level challenges; message design and campaign strategy; risk communication; digital health platforms and telemedicine; confidentiality, regulation and public messaging. Course material may reference real-world health controversies or policy debates as useful for understanding communication processes.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how health, illness and medical practice are represented across media environments, including news, social media, entertainment, advertising and/or public information campaigns. Analyzes how messages about bodies, risk, care, expertise and/or responsibility are constructed and circulated. Considers how media shape public expectations of patients, professionals and/or institutions. Course content may include real-world examples involving sensitive topics such as illness, disability, gender, sexuality, social class and/or race, examined for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to workforce settings in which effective communication about health is essential, including healthcare industries, public relations, nonprofit outreach, journalism and strategic communication. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in health communication, media studies and public health or policy. Strengthens civic media literacy by examining how health information and misinformation spread through media systems, institutional messaging and cultural narratives. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how portrayals of health are shaped not only by medical knowledge but also by narrative conventions, commercial pressures and/or cultural assumptions. Builds understanding of how media depictions of illness, caregiving and wellness can inform, inspire, mislead and/or stigmatize, depending on framing. Facilitates comparison between professional expertise and popular narratives to better understand how public perceptions of health are formed and challenged. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of medical dramas and documentaries; news coverage of disease outbreaks or medical innovation; health marketing and pharmaceutical advertising; public health campaigns and crisis communication; social media communities around wellness, disability or chronic illness; narratives of caregiving and recovery; depictions of healthcare providers and institutions. May include feminist and/or critical approaches to the intersections of health with topics like gender, race and sexuality. Course material may reference real-world historical and contemporary health controversies when useful for understanding communication processes.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the strategic use of social media in professional, organizational and/or public communication contexts. Analyzes how platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn and/or X structure their visibility, engagement and audience expectations. Explores how organizations and individuals craft identity, manage interaction and respond to feedback across different platform cultures. Includes both critical evaluation of existing accounts and hands-on creation of posts, visuals and/or campaigns for specific purposes. Course material may reference real-world social media campaigns related to political, cultural and/or commercial controversy, examined for purposes of communication analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies directly to careers in public relations, branding, journalism, advocacy, content strategy and digital marketing. Builds fluency in platform conventions, analytics, message design and audience targeting; skills applicable in both corporate and nonprofit communication roles. Supports academic growth in media analysis and prepares students for civic participation in increasingly networked communication environments. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how social media operates not only as a tool for promotion but as a space of negotiation between creators, institutions and publics. Highlights differences between personal posting, strategic messaging and algorithmic influence. Informs reflection on the challenges of authenticity, persuasion and accountability when communication is continuous, participatory and highly public. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of platform affordances and algorithmic logics; branding and identity construction; audience engagement strategies; visual and multimedia storytelling; analytics and performance metrics; influencer models and creator economies; platform policy, moderation and crisis response. Course examples may draw from corporate, political, entertainment, activist and/or nonprofit accounts. Content creation components may involve drafting posts, graphics, videos and/or campaign plans in response to simulated or real-world communication goals.
prerequisites: Grade of B or better in COMM 275/JOUR 275 or JOUR 275/COMM 275; junior or senior classification.

description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the role of religious communication in shaping public life through speeches, sermons, debates, campaigns and/or social movements. Considers how religious language, symbols and/or narratives influence cultural identity, moral reasoning and/or collective action. Surveys diverse approaches to studying religious communication, from historical traditions to contemporary debates, highlighting how meaning is constructed, contested and transformed in religious discourse. Considers interpretations of religious communication from multiple perspectives, fostering critical thinking. Explores a diverse range of scholarly frameworks, theories and methods employed in the academic study of religion and religious communication. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Strengthens transferable skills in critical thinking, interpretation and evaluation of persuasive messages in contexts ranging from personal dialogue to civic engagement. Enhances adaptability across diverse religious and cultural frameworks. Supports academic preparation for analyzing communication at the intersection of religion, culture and public life. Engages skills applicable to leadership, education, public study of advocacy and professional fields, when understanding religious perspectives and their influence is relevant. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how religious communication functions not only as a vehicle of belief but also as a force shaping history, politics and/or social change. Provides reflection on ways speeches, symbols and/or campaigns can both unite and divide, reinforcing traditions or sparking transformation. Provides frameworks for critical analysis of religious discourse from first-person and third-person perspectives. Highlights the interpretive challenges posed by pluralism, competing meanings and differing assumptions about authority, sacredness and public expression. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of religious speeches and sermons; debates over doctrine and belief; campaigns and movements shaped by religious rhetoric; analysis of religious symbolism and storytelling; exploration of the role of communication in sustaining or challenging religious traditions. Course materials may address diverse and sometimes controversial perspectives, reflecting the ways religious communication has influenced cultural identity, social conflict and civic life across history.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: Directed individual health communication practicum.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.

description: Directed internship in a public or private organization to provide students with on-the-job training and applied research experience; application of communication theory and practice in career settings; designed to enhance and clarify students' career objectives. May be repeated for credit. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis.
prerequisites: Cumulative GPR of 2.5 or higher for credits taken in residence; approval of department head.

description: Directed individual study of identified topics in communication; may include specific research, readings or other approved project in any area of communication; written report is required. May be repeated for credit.
prerequisites: Cumulative GPR of 2.5 or higher; approval of instructor and department head.

description: Directed individual communication, diversity, social justice capstone experience.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of capstone director.

description: Directed global media experience.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.

description: Selected topics in an identified area of communication. May be repeated for credit.
Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in the department of communication. May be taken four times for credit.
prerequisites: GPA 2.5 or higher; junior or senior classification and approval of instructor and department head.

description: Directed independent studies for upper division Honors students, regardless of academic major, in select aspects of communication. May be repeated for credit.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification either as Honors student or with GPR of 3.25; letter of approval from head of student's department.

description: Basic concepts in using computation to enhance problem solving abilities; understanding how people communicate with computers, and how computing affects society; computational thinking; representation of data; analysis of program behavior; methods for identifying and fixing errors in programs; understanding abilities and limitation of programs; development and execution of programs.

Computation to enhance problem solving abilities; understanding how people communicate with computers, and how computing affects society; computational thinking; software design principles, including algorithm design, data representation, abstraction, modularity, structured and object oriented programming, documentation, testing, portability, and maintenance; understanding programs’ abilities and limitations; development and execution programs.

Extension of prior programming knowledge and creation of computer programs that solve problems; application of computational thinking to enhance problem solving; analysis of, design of and implementation of computer programs; use of basic and aggregate data types; encapsulation and abstraction; development of software that uses dynamic memory and avoids memory leaks; study of error handling strategies to develop more secure and robust programs.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ENGR 102, CSCE 110, CSCE 111, CSCE 206 or PHYS 150.

description: Computation to enhance problem solving abilities; computational thinking; understanding how people communicate with computers, how computing affects society; design and implementation of algorithms; data types, program control, iteration, functions, classes, and exceptions; understanding abstraction, modularity, code reuse, debugging, maintenance, and other aspects of software development; development and execution of programs.
prerequisites: Programming course (high school or college); also taught at Galveston campus.

description: Introduction to the broad field of computing; presentations from industry and academia about how computer science concepts are used in research and end products; includes a major writing component.

Basic terminology, concepts, technology, and trends of cybersecurity; foundations of cybersecurity to include cryptography, public key infrastructure, standards and protocols, physical security, network fundamentals; workings of systems, networks, infrastructure; legal and ethical issues in cybersecurity.

Basic concepts, nomenclature and historical perspective of computers and computing; internal representation of data; software design principles and practice; structured and object-oriented programming in C; use of terminals, operation of editors and executions of student-written programs.

Specification and implementation of basic abstract data types and their associated algorithms including stacks, queues, lists, sorting and selection, searching, graphs and hashing; performance tradeoffs of different implementations and asymptotic analysis of running time and memory usage.
prerequisites: Grade C or better in CSCE 120 or CSCE 121; grade of C or better in CSCE 222 or ECEN 222, or concurrent enrollment.

description: Mathematical foundations from discrete mathematics for analyzing computer algorithms, for both correctness and performance; introduction to models of computation, including finite state machines and Turing machines.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 142, MATH 147, MATH 151, or MATH 171.

description: Introduction to legal, social and ethical issues in computing and software development; emphasizes ethical decision-making, professional responsibility and communication, with coverage of professional codes, organizational ethics, law and policy, intellectual property, open-source software and variety of contemporary topics.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221; also taught at Galveston campus.

description: Special project in computer science; project must be approved by the department.
prerequisites: Approval of department head; also taught at Galveston campus.

description: Selected topics in an identified area of computer science. May be repeated for credit.
prerequisites: Approval of instructor.

description: Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in computer science. May be taken three times for credit.
prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor.

description: Computational practice of data science through a sequence of interactive modules that provides an integrated hands-on approach to its methods, tools, applications and supporting technologies including high performance and cloud computing platforms.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ENGR 102, CSCE 110, CSCE 111, or CSCE 206; grade of C or better in MATH 251, MATH 253, or STAT 211; junior or senior classification.

description: File structures and access methods; database modeling, design and user interface; components of database management systems; information storage and retrieval, query languages, high-level language interface with database systems.
prerequisites: CSCE 221 with a grade of C or better; junior or senior classification.

description: Computer systems from programmer's perspective including simple logic design, data representation and processor architecture, programming of processors, memory, control flow, input/output, and performance measurements; hands-on lab assignments.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221, or concurrent enrollment.

description: Introduction to system support for application programs, both on single node and over network including OS application interface, inter-process communication, introduction to system and network programming, and simple computer security concepts; hands-on lab assignments.
prerequisites: CSCE 221 with a grade of C or better; grade of C or better in CSCE 312 or concurrent enrollment in CSCE 350/ECEN 350 or ECEN 350/CSCE 350.

description: Exploration of the design space of programming languages via an in-depth study of functional and object-oriented programming concepts, using concrete programming languages as examples. Focuses on idiomatic uses of programming language constructs and on features characteristic for each language.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221, or concurrent enrollment.

description: Intensive programming experience that integrates core concepts in Computer Science and familiarizes with a variety of programming/development tools and techniques; students work on 2 or 3 month-long projects each emphasizing a different specialization within Computer Science; focuses on programming techniques to ease code integration, reusability, and clarity.
prerequisites: CSCE 312 and CSCE 314, or CSCE 350/ECEN 350 or ECEN 350/CSCE 350; concurrent enrollment in CSCE 313.

description: Theoretical foundations, algorithms and methods of deriving valuable insights from data; includes foundations in managing and analyzing data at scale, e.g. big data; data mining techniques and algorithms; exploratory data analysis; statistical methods and models; data visualization.
prerequisites: STAT 211 or ECEN 303; STAT 212 or CSCE 222; MATH 304.

description: Foundations of artificial intelligence and machine learning; search, reasoning and knowledge representation; planning, decision making and problem solving; supervised and unsupervised learning; deep learning methods and generative AI; applications across domains such as language, vision and robotics; evaluation of systems; ethical and societal implications.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221 and CSCE 222; grade of C or better in STAT 211 or ECEN 303; also taught at Galveston campus.

description: Intensive programming experience and provision of the fundamentals needed for larger-scale software development; integration of concepts in computer science and familiarization with a variety of programming and development tools and techniques; team projects each with an emphasis on a different specialization within computer science; emphasis on programming techniques to ease code integration and clarity; practical exposure to software-engineering processes through large-scale projects and specification and documentation.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 314, CSCE 350/ECEN 350, or ECEN 350/CSCE 350; grade of C or better or concurrent enrollment in CSCE 313.

description: Computer architecture and design; use of register transfer languages and simulation tools to describe and simulate computer operation; central processing unit organization, input/output and memory system architectures.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECEN 248 and CSCE 120; junior or senior classification.

description: Participation in an approved high-impact learning practice; documentation and self-assessment of learning experience.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

description: Examination of law and policy issues related to cybersecurity for the spectrum of cybersecurity jobs; includes procurement, operations and maintenance, governance and oversight, protection and defense, analysis, intelligence collection and operation and investigation cybersecurity jobs.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; MARA-403 taught at Galveston campus.

description: Hardware/software evolution leading to contemporary operating systems; basic operating systems concepts; methods of operating systems design and construction including algorithms for CPU scheduling, memory and general resource allocation, process coordination and management; case studies of several operating systems.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 313; grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331.

description: Study of computer algorithms for numeric and non-numeric problems; design paradigms; analysis of time and space requirements of algorithms; correctness of algorithms; NP-completeness and undecidability of problems.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221 and CSCE 222; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: Operating system and distributed systems fields that form the basis of cloud computing such as virtualization, key-value storage solutions, group membership, failure detection, peer to peer systems, datacenter networking, resource management and scalability; popular frameworks such as MapReduce and HDFS and case studies on failure determination.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331.

description: Basic principles of design and implementation of defect-free software, code reviews including tool-assisted review by static and dynamic analysis, risk analysis and management and methods for software security testing.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331; or approval of instructor.

description: Hardware functional verification; case studies on verification in integrated circuit design; introduction to industry best practices; introduction to logic functional verification.
prerequisites: CSCE 312, CSCE 350/ECEN 350, or ECEN 350/CSCE 350, or equivalent in computer architecture; familiarity with C/C++/Verilog/VHDL programming.

description: Fundamental concepts and techniques of intelligent systems; representation and interpretation of knowledge on a computer; search strategies and control; active research areas and applications such as notational systems, natural language understanding, vision systems, planning algorithms, intelligent agents and expert systems.
prerequisites: CSCE 411 or approval of instructor.

description: Theoretical foundations of machine learning, pattern recognition and generating predictive models and classifiers from data; includes methods for supervised and unsupervised learning (decision trees, linear discriminants, neural networks, Gaussian models, non-parametric models, clustering, dimensionality reduction, deep learning), optimization procedures and statistical inference.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 304, MATH 311, or MATH 323; Grade of C or better in STAT 211, and STAT 404 or CSCE 221, or ECEN 303, and CSCE 121 or CSCE 120.

description: Software development cycle; software outsourcing model, execution and practices; software industries on products, services and consultancy; software globalization; and offshore development culture; travel abroad required.
prerequisites: CSCE 315 or approval of instructor.

description: Methods for analyzing fundamental programming problems from a variety of domains and implementing solutions quickly and efficiently; problems based on competitive programming contests to develop skills in problem analysis, coding and testing; solving problems will involve identifying and applying a range of algorithmic solutions; includes dealing with combinatorics, dynamic programming, graphs, numerical calculations, string processing and geometry, along with other specialized algorithms.
prerequisites: CSCE 411 or approval of instructor.

description: Application of engineering approach to computer software design and development; life cycle models, software requirements and specification; conceptual model design; detailed design; validation and verification; design quality assurance; software design/development environments and project management.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 or approval of instructor.

description: Exploration of the characteristics of traditionally disenfranchised user populations due to disability including discrimination; universal design concepts; exploration of ethical and legal motivations for creating accessible technology; development, evaluation, design, and implementation of equitable and inclusive software and computer based solutions; study of multiple existing accessibility standards.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331.

description: Basic types of abstract languages and their acceptors; the Chomsky hierarchy; solvability and recursive function theory; application of theoretical results to practical problems.
prerequisites: CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 or approval of instructor.

description: Programming language translation; functions and general organization of compiler design and interpreters; theoretical and implementation aspects of lexical scanners; parsing of context free languages; code generation and optimization; error recovery.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331.

description: Overview of parallel computing technology and programming methods; includes multiprocessor architectures, programming tools, parallel performance, parallel algorithms, and applications of parallel computing.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: Comprehensive study of the Computer-Human Interaction (CHI) area; includes history and importance of CHI; CHI design theories; modeling of computer users and interfaces; empirical techniques for task analysis and interface design; styles of interaction and future directions of CHI including hypermedia and computer-supported collaborative work.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 or concurrent enrollment; or approval of instructor.

description: Principles and techniques for engineering distributed systems with topics including communication, concurrency, programming paradigms, naming, managing shared state, caching, synchronization, reaching agreement, fault tolerance, security, middleware and distributed applications; design, implement and debug large software systems.
prerequisites: CSCE 313; junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

description: Theoretical foundations, algorithms and methods of data analytics for cybersecurity; study of data analytics including cluster analysis, supervised machine learning, anomaly detection, and visualization applied to cyber attacks, anomaly detection, vulnerability analysis, strategic manipulation, propaganda and other topics.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 221; grade of C or better in ECEN 303, STAT 211, STAT 301, STAT 302, or STAT 303.

description: Introduction to the design and analysis of quantum algorithms; basic principles of the quantum circuit model; gives a gentle introduction to basic quantum algorithms; reviews recent results in quantum information processing.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 or approval of instructor.

description: Principles of interactive computer graphics; 2-D and 3-D rendering pipelines, including geometric object and view transformations, projections, hidden surface removal, and rasterization; lighting models for local and global illumination; hierarchical models of 3-D objects; systems and libraries supporting display and user interaction.
prerequisites: CSCE 221; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: Introduction to numerical algorithms fundamental to scientific and engineering applications of computers; elementary discussion of error; algorithms, efficiency; polynomial approximations, quadrature and systems of algebraic and differential equations.
prerequisites: CSCE 221 with a grade of C or better; MATH 304 or MATH 308 or concurrent enrollment.

description: Aesthetic and technical aspects of computer game development, including game mechanics, story development, content creation and game programming; includes game design, interface design, 3D modeling and animation, graphics algorithms, shader programming and artificial intelligence; group project includes the design and development of a game from start to finish.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in VIST 386 or CSCE 441, or approval of instructor.

description: A systems approach to the programming, design, authoring and theory of hypermedia; object-oriented visual and interactive programming; visual design, including color, space, text and layering; the reference as a metadisciplinary structure; collecting and sampling; ontologies, maps and navigation as means of structuring information; create dynamic hypermedia that is expressive and interpretive.
prerequisites: CSCE 315 or approval of instructor.

description: Potential and realized impact of computers in the design of new media; relationship between authors and readers of interactive material; influence of media design on the content expressed.
prerequisites: CSCE 221 or approval of instructor.

description: Theory and practice of virtual reality; interactive 3D virtual environments; input/output devices, 3D interaction techniques, augmented reality, role of realism in VR, navigation techniques, design guidelines and evaluation methods.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in VIST 272, CSCE 221, or CSCE 441.

description: Visual representation and design of data and information; 3D visualization, infographics, data narratives, principles of visual data encoding and interaction techniques.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in VIST 272, or CSCE 221, or CSCE 441.

description: Cameras and the image formation process; basic image and video processing tools like sampling, filtering and pyramids; several image-based algorithms, including panorama creation, lightfields, image retargeting, high dynamic range imaging and texture synthesis.
prerequisites: CSCE 315 or CSCE 331; MATH 304 or MATH 311.

description: A comprehensive overview of the theory and practice of securing systems through cryptography. Topics include foundational security design principles, attacker models, classical ciphers and secure randomness; modern symmetric-key (stream and block) and asymmetric/public-key ciphers; cryptographic primitives including hash functions, digital signatures, message authentication codes and key exchange. Applications are explored, along with emerging trends. Hands-on projects provide practical experience with cryptographic tools.
prerequisites: CSCE 221.

description: Investigation of computational problems in computer animation; study of the mathematical and algorithmic foundations behind various techniques used for computer animation for real-time and offline use.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331; grade of C or better in or concurrent enrollment in CSCE 441.

description: Overview of the compilation mechanism to generate executable files and raw binary codes from source codes; executable file formats for an operating system to run the binary code; disassembly algorithms and control graph analysis; static and dynamic analyses; case studies on code obfuscation, codebreaking, malware analysis.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 313 or approval of instructor.

description: Algorithms for executing spatial tasks; path planning and obstacle aance in two- and three-dimensional robots--configuration space, potential field, free-space decomposition methods; stable grasping and manipulation; dealing with uncertainty; knowledge representation for planning--geometric and symbolic models of the environment; task-level programming; learning.
prerequisites: CSCE 315 or CSCE 331; MATH 304 or MATH 311.

description: Microcomputers as components of systems; VLSI processor and coprocessor architectures, addressing and instruction sets; I/O interfaces and supervisory control; VLSI architectures for signal processing; integrating special purpose processors into a system.
prerequisites: CSCE 313.

description: Basic hardware/software and architectural components for computer communications; delay, loss, throughput and topology of packet networks; application/transport-layer protocols, network-layer routing, data-link switching; security; socket programming, kernel APIs and multi-threading; case studies of existing networks, protocols and architectures.
prerequisites: CSCE 313 or approval of instructor.

description: Introduction to wireless and mobile systems; wireless communication fundamentals; wireless medium access control design; transmission scheduling, network and transport protocols over wireless design, simulation and evaluation; wireless capacity; telecommunication systems; vehicular, adhoc, and sensor network systems; wireless security; mobile applications.
prerequisites: CSCE 313; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: Fundamental concepts and principles of computer security, operating system and network security, secret key and public key cryptographic algorithms, hash functions, authentication, firewalls and intrusion detection systems, IPSec and VPN, wireless and web security.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331, and CSCE 313; junior or senior classification; approval of instructor.

description: Advanced computer architectures including memory designs, pipeline techniques and parallel structures such as out-of-order cores and multiprocessors.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECEN 350/CSCE 350 or CSCE 350/ECEN 350; junior or senior classification.

description: Representation of, storage of and access to very large multimedia document collections; fundamental data structures and algorithms of current information storage and retrieval systems and relates various techniques to design and evaluation of complete retrieval systems.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331 or approval of instructor.

description: NLP fundamentals including word semantics, language models, discourse and pragmatics; introduction to various applications including information extraction, sentiment analysis, question and answering, text summarization and machine translation.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 331 or approval of instructor; junior or senior classification.

description: Risks in cybersecurity; avoidance, acceptance, mitigation, or transference strategies; developing reliable cybersecurity risk assessments to include analysis, categorization, and evaluation; cybersecurity risk audit frameworks.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CYBR 201/CSCE 201, CSCE 201/CYBR 201, or CSCE 221; junior or senior classification.

description: Investigation and report by students on topics of current interest in computer science.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: Development of system integration skills for solving real-world problems in computer science; significant team software project that uses integration of advanced concepts across computer science specializations; projects require design, implementation, documentation and demonstration, as well as design methodology, management process and teamwork.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 411, and CSCE 315 or CSCE 331; senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

description: Engineering design; working as a design-team member, conceptual design methodology, design evaluations, total project planning and management techniques, design optimization, systems manufacturing costs considerations; emphasis placed upon students' activities as design professionals.
prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CSCE 315 or CSCE 331, and CSCE 462 or ECEN 449, and ECEN 325; senior classification.

description: Permits work on special project in computer science; project must be approved by the department.
prerequisites: Senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

description: Special topics in computer science that are new or unique that are not covered in existing courses.
Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in computer science. May be taken four times for credit.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.

description: Intensive study of and practice in writing processes, from invention and researching to drafting, revising and editing, both individually and corroboratively; emphasis on effective rhetorical choices including audience, purpose, arrangement and style; focus on writing the academic essay as a vehicle for learning, communicating and critical analysis.

Focus on written communication through the development of analytical reading ability, critical thinking and information literacy; emphasis on effective rhetorical choices such as audience, purpose, arrangement and style. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification; also taught at Galveston and Qatar campuses.

description: How does one tell the story of the natural world and human interactions within it? This course explores that question through environmental literature, investigating creative efforts that imagine, celebrate, exploit and advocate for the more-than-human world. Students will engage with a variety of texts, practice interpretive methods from literary studies and ask critical questions about how narrative and other forms of representation shape our understanding of the environment and our personal or social responsibilities to the natural world of which humans are a part. This course is reading intensive. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives; also taught at Qatar campus.

Focus on writing about literature through practice in skills such as literary analysis, close reading and interpretation; practice in writing, discussion and other forms of communication about texts; may include works drawn from a wide range of definitions of literature, such as novels, films, songs, poetry, drama and/or other kinds of texts. Text selection organized thematically and/or by genre. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives; also taught at Galveston campus.

Introduction to literature by African Americans emphasizing major themes and traditions. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. ENGL-204 also taught at Galveston campus.

This course covers a variety of cultural texts (individual works, literary movements, genres and so forth) by authors of African descent in Africa, Europe and the Americas. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.

Introduction to some of the major literary and cultural forms of the twenty-first century. Course topics might include texts from a variety of national and cultural origins, different approaches to a relevant topic or representations of contemporary historical events. Students will explore how contemporary aesthetic and intellectual texts develop and express ideas about the human condition across cultures. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives; also taught at Qatar campus.

Introduction to digital culture(s); exposure to some methodologies for the interpretation and critique of digital media from the humanities. These may include but are not limited to approaches from critical data studies, media studies, digital humanities, and the history of science and technology. Students can expect to gain experience analyzing digital media and expect to develop critical thinking and intercultural competence while engaging in respectful discourse on complex topics related to digital cultures. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
Nature of human language and of linguistics; includes an introduction to phonology, syntax, semantics and morphology and the role of spoken and written discourse in sustaining societal arrangements.

Focus on writing for technical and professional rhetorical situations with an emphasis on document design, audience awareness, clarity of communication and collaborative teamwork. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives; also taught at Galveston and Qatar campuses.

Introduction to history, influence and major ideas of Cultural Studies; use of culture as a means to critique social problems and understand social forces; analysis of culture in its relationship to power; participation in project investigating contemporary U.S. youth subcultures.

Exploration of selected works of Shakespeare in text, performance and/or adaptation, with attention to various historical, cultural and/or political contexts informing Shakespeare’s texts and their study. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives; also taught at Galveston campus.

Exploration of the interrelationships of literature and other arts, including the exchange or adaptation of aesthetic principles, techniques and content among textual, visual and multimedia art forms, such as painting, sculpture, film, music, architecture, graphic and decorative arts. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives; also taught at Qatar campus.

An exploration of the graphic novel as a medium, with a focus on the form’s varieties, use of both textual and visual elements and impacts on our understanding of storytelling and artistic expression; analysis of texts in relation to social and cultural contexts, various theoretical lenses and/or scholarly engagements with graphic novels. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.

World Literature I. Survey of world literature from the ancient world through the sixteenth century in relation to its historical and cultural contexts; texts selected from a broad group of authors, traditions and genres. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. ENGL-221 also taught at Qatar campus.

World Literature II. Survey of world literature from the seventeenth century to the present in relation to its historical and cultural contexts; texts selected from a broad group of authors, traditions and genres. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. ENGL-222 also taught at Galveston and Qatar campuses.

This course is a survey introduction to American literature from the beginnings of the Americas to the Civil War examining writers, genres and movements of the period. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.

This course is a survey introduction to American literature from the Civil War to the present examining writers, genres and movements of the period. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.

Introduction to the historical scope of Asian American literature and culture, primarily though not limited to writing and cultural artifacts from the late 19th century to the present. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.

Literature of England from the early medieval period through the 18th century, with attention to various historical, cultural and/or political contexts informing the texts and their study. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.

Literature of Great Britain and its colonies from the late 18th century to the 21st century, with attention to various historical, cultural, political and/or critical contexts informing the texts and their study. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives; also taught at Qatar campus.

Introduction to the speculative and marvelous genres of literature; survey of genres such as science fiction, fantasy, horror, fairy tales and/or related media such as film with their respective genre concepts, narrative frameworks and significant authors and directors; examination of different methodological approaches and historical contexts. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.

Initiation into the craft of creative writing in prose and poetry; extensive reading in the genres; peer workshops. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent published creative work and satisfy course learning objectives.

Focus on and practice in the writing of advanced academic and/or professional prose. May consider topics such as scholarly genres of writing and/or questions related to writing process, research, style, audience awareness, digital writing or ethics in scholarly discourse. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. Also taught at Galveston campus.
Fundamental aspects of film analysis and criticism; ENGL-251 also taught at Galveston and Qatar campuses.

Introduction to Cultural Studies and Popular Cultural. An introduction to the history, theories and methods of contemporary cultural studies. The course will explore key concepts in cultural theory to examine specific aspects of popular culture as well as cultural sites and practices so as to expand upon the analytical and critical thinking skills learned in ENGL 104 and 203.
prerequisites: ENGL 104; Galveston campus.

description: Introduction to Latinx literature and cultural production; emphasis on methods and approaches, historical breadth and context and the diverse literary traditions of people of Hispanic and Latinx descent throughout the United States and the Americas. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
Readings selected for specific need of major or minor in English.
Selected topics in an identified area of English. May be repeated for credit.
Research conducted under the direction of faculty member in English.
prerequisites: 3 hours of 200-level literature; freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor.

description: Introduction to methodology, scope and practice of literature and medicine studies; analysis of literature and/or other texts dealing with health and illness; engagement with different disciplinary perspectives as a tool for critical thinking. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.

A writing intensive introduction to the central methods of the discipline and the operations of the major at Texas A&M. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: ENGL 104 or concurrent enrollment; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: Examination of a particular digital theme, genre or technology from a humanities perspective, such as introduction to making and/or interpreting digital materials; study of digital culture and/or digital archives. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. May be taken three times for credit.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

description: Examination of Texas literature, culture and multi-media; exploration of the development of Texas identities and responses to the rich cultural expressions within the state; topics vary with each section. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: Examination of texts written in English that de-center the nation-state as the central way to organize cultural comparison; includes colonialism, economics, empire, globalization, migration, race and refugees. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Qatar campus.

description: History of critical thought about art and culture from antiquity to the present; topics and readings span a variety of eras, approaches and artistic genres. Key themes and ideas in criticism may be presented in the context of historical figures or entire critical movements such as new criticism, structuralism and poststructuralism, historical materialism, feminism, race and ethnic studies and cultural studies, among others. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent historic and current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above.

description: Exploration of the concept of cultural politics across several academic disciplines in the humanities and social sciences; broad interrogation of relationships that mediate culture and power in national and international contexts; focus on how culture shapes and is shaped by society, political perspectives and actions.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; or approval of the instructor.

description: Phonological, grammatical and lexical history of the English language; brief discussion of some other Indo-European languages; principles of linguistic change, as reflected in English in relation to its historical and cultural contexts. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: Introductory study of Old and Middle English literature, exclusive of Chaucer, surveying major genres and topics. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above.

description: Period course in the poetry, prose and drama of the intellectual and artistic movement known as the Renaissance, which flourished in England throughout the 16th and early 17th centuries. Additional attention will be given to historical, cultural and/or political contexts informing the texts and their study. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above.

description: Period course in English poetry, prose and drama of the 17th century with attention to various historical, cultural and/or political contexts informing the texts and their study. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above.

description: Period course studying literature written in English created during the “long” 18th century (1660-1820) with attention given to its cultural contexts. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above.

description: Period course in early British, non-Shakespearean drama to 1642 with attention to various historical, cultural and/or political contexts informing early drama and its study. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at the 200-level or above.

description: Exploration of historical and contemporary utopian literature through a variety of writers and texts. Topics may include but are not limited to: the relationship between utopia and dystopia; various critical theories related to utopia, dystopia and/or planning for the “good life”; myriad developments of the genre in relationship to developments of politics, history, culture and/or literary study. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above.

description: Focus on the practice of principles and methods of technical and professional editing across print and digital media, including copyediting, comprehensive editing and editorial project management with attention to standards, style and design. Topics may include understanding rhetorical situations of editing projects; editing for organization, clarity, accuracy, grammar and usability; and collaboration with writers and editors. Students can expect to strengthen skills in critical thinking, written communication and professional collaboration while developing an understanding of the role of editors in contemporary workplaces. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: ENGL 210.

description: Representative texts in English generated throughout the British empire in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, with attention to the cultural and historical contexts that produced them. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above.

description: Exploration of some representative works of literature by writers resident in Great Britain and its colonies during the Victorian period. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above.

description: Period course in American literature and culture from the 1820s to the 1860s, covering writers who may include, but not limited to, Emerson, Hawthorne, Thoreau, Walker, Douglass, Melville, Poe, Whitman, Dickinson, Jacobs and others. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above.

description: History and trajectory of science fiction cinema into the 21st century by significant filmmakers, attending to film theory and genre studies; historical, aesthetic and technical developments; and the cultural and philosophical issues of the films. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above.

description: This course includes writers, genres and movements in the African American literary tradition from the beginnings through the Harlem Renaissance studied within cultural and historical context. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: 3 credits of literature at 200-level or above.

description: Legend of King Arthur in the original language or translation from its Medieval origins to the present. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that are represented in current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

description: An exploration of the development of the fantasy genre which may include a survey of foundational texts (medieval romance, myth, fairy tales, etc.) and such topics as significant authors, movements, sub-genres and media. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: LGBTQ texts studied in their cross-cultural, historical, political contexts. Topics may include but are not limited to studies in camp, authorship, (mis)representations in popular culture, the closet and queer coding, queer visual and performance cultures; race, sex, empire. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

description: Origins and development of the science fiction genre. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

description: Significance of the sea in fictional and factual accounts, such as novels, short stories, poems and narratives of sailors and seafaring life.
prerequisites: Three credits of literature at 200 level or above; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; Galveston campus; also taught at College Station campus.

description: The Southwestern region of the United States is a complicated place of competing values and cultures and peoples. In this class we will read novels and view films and artwork by Southwestern writers and artists, and we will discuss the ways these works do — or do not — reflect the complex ways in which we define the Southwest and America. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives.
prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.
